articleTitle: Reverse Energy Transfer through an AC Line Synchronized Pulse Width Modulated Sinewave Inverter
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Pulse width modulated inverters are used in battery supplied systems as AC standby power sources to supply high quality sinewaves to critical loads. In all these systems, means must be provided for battery charging. The traditional method uses a separate rectifier to charge the battery. A pulse width modulated four-quadrant inverter can be made to pass power in either direction, functioning as a synchronous rectifier to provide complete control for all battery charging requirements. In its simplest form, the charging scheme can be modelled as two synchronous AC voltage sources separated by an inductor. Power transfer is effected when one voltage source differs in amplitude and phase from the other. This report describes the basic theory of line synchronized inverter operation and the realization of this theory using a pulse width modulated inverter operating as a closed-loop switching amplifier. The piece-wise linear time domain analysis of actual inverter waveforms to battery charging conditions are presented. This analysis details the instantaneous energy flow into the battery during a full cycle of utility sinewave. System trade-offs to realize a cost-effective product are identified and discussed. Waveforms, system performance, and applications are presented.

articleTitle: A New Family of Switched Mode Rectifiers
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: A new family of Switched Mode Rectifiers (SMR's) is described. These SMR's each utilize a common power train concept, range in power from 125 W to 500 W and are used to power switching, transmission and subscriber equipment. In each application specific modifications are incorporated resulting in an optimum cost/performance trade-off for each design. When compared to conventional (SCR or ferroresonant) rectifiers the SMR's offer 5% increase in efficiency and 50% reduction in size and weight.

articleTitle: High-Efficiency Switching Regulator using Sub Class E Switching Mode
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: A high efficiency switching dc-to-dc converter is presented, which operates at about 100 kHz with an ordinary bipolar transistor. A new converter is based on the buck converter. By positively taking advantage of the switching transistor output capacitance and the transformer leakage inductance, it is possible to realize little switching loss. When the "off" state transient response reaches zero voltage across the switching transistor, before the beginning of the "on" state, it does so with approximately zero slope. To maintain the above-mentioned operation mode, it is necessary that Ton/T of the transistor, primary inductance Lp, leakage inductance Le and the sum of the transistor output capacitance and the external capacitance are strictly selected by numerical analysis. An example is given of the new converter design to deliver a continuous power of 100 W at about 100 kHz with an overall system efficiency greater than 90 percent into a variable load. Further, unwanted noise is not produced.

articleTitle: Computer and Non-Linear Load Applications of Uninterruptible Power Supplies
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: In the application of U.P.S. to computer loads, the transient performance criteria of some computers has led to the assumption that a fast acting inverter is the ultimate aim of the designer. Fast-acting inverters use either pulse-width modulation or waveform synthesis to eliminate low order harmonics and are typified by a relatively cheap small output filter. In contrast other inverters have large filters and may also have trap circuits to eliminate specific harmonics. It is not always appreciated that the use of a small filter aggregates the problem of harmonic distortion and overloading when the inverter has a non-linear load. Since most computer and industrial loads contain a.c. to d.c. power supplies which are non-linear in their loading characteristics, the effect is prevalent and can be observed as waveform distortion and current pulsing of the inverter output.

articleTitle: Stored-Program Control of DC Power Plants
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: This paper reports on an experimental computer-based data acquisition and control system for central office dc power plants. In this experiment, a microcomputer monitors the alarms and operational status of the rectifiers, batteries and distribution network which comprise the power plant. The microcomputer's control of the power plant is aimed at maximizing the efficiency of the plant by turning rectifiers on and off depending on the office load and the condition of the commercial ac input. The algorithm for controlling the rectifiers also equalizes their operating times and accounts for limited output capability due to ac phase failures. Additional computations are done to determine the net ampere-hour reserve available from the batteries based on the net charge flow into the batteries. Administration of the data available in the plant involves recording battery, rectifier and fuse alarms and critical voltages and currents in calendar time. A record of these events is used to deduce probable causes of troubles and to anticipate repair times, plant growth and feeder additions. This data is formatted and made available to an office control center or remote terminal. The hardware for the experimental system is configured using a DEC 11/03 Microcomputer and Hewlett-Packard Multiprogrammer, Scanner and Digital Multimeter interconnected on an IEEE 488 Bus. The software is written in C Language using the UNIX* operating system. The program structure uses a hardware clock interrupt to invoke measurement and control routines at prescribed intervals in calendar time.

articleTitle: The Development of a Lightweight, Modular, Sinewave Inverter System Eliminating Common Control and Low Frequency Transformation
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The British Post Office (BPO) and ERA Technology Ltd have developed a new concept in modular inverter systems by combining expertise from an earlier development with inverters to a novel ERA design. Modules can be paralleled to suit different loads, and reliability can be increased by the further addition of active redundant modules. The new inverters produce a high efficiency 50 Hz sinewave output without the use of iron-cored components. The modules do not require a master control for synchronisation and also incorporate a facility to switch the load between the inverter output and an alternative a.c. supply.

articleTitle: A New Generation of Stationary Lead-Acid Batteries for Telecommunications
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Several authors at the INTELEC '79 meeting reported that Lead-Acid batteries would provide the dominant power reserve for telecommunications in the future. The demands made upon the batteries would be similar to those of today, notably reliability in standby. But some new demands must be met, such as freedom from maintenance, full insulation and ease of installation and commissioning. Beside existing standard types with either tubular or Planté plates we describe a new family of cells with capacities ranging from 12,5 Ah to 600 Ah. The main features of these cells, which were introduced into the market some few years ago, are as follows: - 6 V, 4 V, and 2 V modules, 12,5 Ah to 600 Ah. - Capacities above 600 Ah in preparation. - Delivered pre-charged and fully dried in sealed packages. - Fully insulated, flexible inter-cell connectors. - Gas tight pole seals. - Ready for immediate use after filling with electrolyte. - Maintenance intervals of 3 years. - Low voltage drop, optimised inter-cell connectors. - Low self discharge, corrosion resistant Selenium alloy grids. - Suited to both standby and cycling use where erratic power supplies cause these conditions. - Flame retardant plugs. This new battery family is truly designed for general purpose applications.

articleTitle: Transistorized Low-Power Power Plant for Telecommunication Systems
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: This paper deals with a power plant designed to provide a no-break 48 or 60 V nominal DC voltage to traditional and technically advanced telecommunication equipment to supply power ratings of up to 300 A. The power plant uses the basic circuit which was chosen by SIP, Italian Telephone Company, for medium and large power plants (1) and was designed to meet the requirements deriving from the decentralization of supplied loads optimizing the overall efficiency of the power supply system. A description of the power plant equipment will be given for rectifiers, buck-boost converters, etc. and for the use of 20kHz PWM power transistor switchers to control the DC output. System engineering will also be described, as well as the expandibility of the plant using standard modules of different power rating.

articleTitle: The Introduction of an Automatic Standby AC Power Plant for Rural Telephone Exchanges
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Over recent years it became evident that there would be a requirement for a small AC, single phase, automatic power plant to improve the operating power reserves of the small rural telephone exchange under extended mains failure conditions. These exchanges make up half of the 6300 telephone exchanges in the United Kingdom network. The present range of larger packaged power plants, installed in medium sized exchanges, were not considered suitable to be adapted to operate in existing buildings. This paper explains the background to the design and development of this new power plant.

articleTitle: Cooling System for Electronic Telephone Exchanges
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Electronic switching systems feature high packing density and high heat density compared with electro-mechanical equipment. Consequently the importance of the cooling system has increased considerably. The climate in a switching room must be kept within specified values under all operational circumstances, including mains failure. Further requirements are: high operational reliability, no special demands on space or the layout of the building, extendability, simple installation and minimal maintenance. This paper describes a cooling system designed specially for electronic switching centers. The system uses water as a heat transfer medium, in contrast to conventional air based cooling systems.

articleTitle: Microprocessors in Power Control, The Time has Come
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Historically, ac reserve power systems have been limited to relay logic controls; and while some evolution into solid state controls has been realized, in general these controllers have replaced relay logic on a function-to-function basis with only limited improvement in features. With the advent of small, low cost and highly reliable microcomputer circuitry, the designer can look beyond the standard control functions of a standby system and consider integrating the processing power of the microcomputer into other aspects of the building power systems. A design example of a real-time microprocessor based controller for standby diesel alternators in a telecommunication environment will be presented. Emphasis will be placed on development considerations such as control functions necessary, hardware chosen and software implementation. The following features of the controller will also be discussed: Flexibility - The concept of functional reconfiguration whereby a single control board can be utilized in different applications via software changes. Testability - Onboard self-diagnostics for field service and interfacing with automated production test equipment. Expandability - Bus oriented structure as a vehicle for expanding processor power to other applications and multiprocessor interface. The single board microprocessor based controller is presently in production, and its base objectives of reduced cost, increased reliability and testability over its sequential logic counterparts have been realized.

articleTitle: Grounding Techniques in Bell System Central Offices
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: For decades, the field of grounding in central office installation was a neglected art. Since 1960, as more sophisticated circuitry is applied to telephone switching and supporting operations, grounding is being increasingly recognized as an important consideration. Effective grounding is necessary to maintain equalization of potential throughout the ground plane of the system, to minimize impedance produced electrical noise and to afford adequate protection to equipment and personnel. In the Bell System, grounding design has evolved from a rudimentary system that depended greatly on incidental conductivity through cable racks, frame metal and other metallic objects. In modern central offices that rudimentary system has been augmented by a Central Office Grounding (CO GRD) system that effectively extends the office ground electrode to every floor of the building to provide a convenient low impedance point of grounding reference. The CO GRD system is horizontally extended on each floor to every frame. The system is designed to limit normal difference of potential between any two point on the ground plane of the building to less than one-half volt difference. Electronic Switching Systems (ESS) in the Bell System have employed a single point ground system to protect the solid-state circuitry from transient-voltage damage since the inception of ESS. Experience has indicated that the relatively modest-cost system has proved to be reliable and effective in keeping disruption of service and equipment damage to an acceptable minimum. This paper describes the techniques employed to establish a CO GRD system and an ESS single point ground system.

articleTitle: A Resonant Converter with PWM Control
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: A dc-to-dc converter of resonant type regulated by PWM means is presented. The converter consists of two stages. The first stage is the boost converter with a switch of MOS FET. The change of the output voltage is regulated by this switch. The second stage is the self-oscillating inverter with rectified output. In the dc side of the output rectifier, a parallel capacitor is connected. A resonant condition is satisfied between the capacitor and the leakage inductance of the inverter transformer. The resonant frequency is almost the same as that of the oscillating frequency. With the resonance phenomena, the switching loss of the transistor is decreased. A good regulation is obtained by the feedback from the output to the boost converter.

articleTitle: New DC Power Supply System
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: A new DC power supply system is under development. The 150V DC power supply system is suitable for digital telecommunications systems. In the 150V system, since bulk DC-DC converters are necessary to supply 48V power, the bulk converter system configuration was investigated. To meet the overload caused by heavy traffic congestion and to assure higher reliability than conventional power supply systems, it is effective to compose the bulk converter system of n+2 units and to install a 48V bypass feeder from a part of the 150V batteries to 48V loads in case of local exchange bulk converter system. A grounding method for noise suppression in the converter output has also been investigated. It clarified that a one point grounding method should be introduced and the out-put ground terminal for each converter should be grounded with a cable separately from the main distribution cable. The 150V system gives 45% space saving, 35% energy saving and 30% cost reduction for the digital switching system power supply, as compared with a conventional 48V system.

articleTitle: A New Hybrid UPS Inverter
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of a unique new static inverter for incorporation into an uninterruptible power system. In inverter design and configuration, overall performance is a compromise between various parameters such as range of DC input voltage, output impedance, transient response of voltage to load changes and input source changes & total harmonic distortion. This inverter concept is in effect a combination of pulse width modulation and stepwave designs. In this way it maintains a good measure of the transient capability and load compatability of the former with the high efficiency of the latter. This is further enhanced by the use of high voltage DC. It has been found to be a more optimum approach to the mid power range UPS systems, typically rated around 250 KVA. Illustrations of inverter systems of this type are presented and comparisons are made to other contemporary techniques.

articleTitle: Photovoltaic Systems as Energy Source for Telecom Equipment
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The introduction of new decentralized telecom equipment using digital techniques such as concentrators, PCM-equipment, etc;, with an insignificant power consumption is taking place. Together with the prospects of a pronounced fall in prices of solar cells within this decade this has caused Jutland Telephone to consider the possibility of using solar cell/battery systems in the primary energy supply for some of this new telecom equipment. Two stand-alone photovoltaic pilot plants were established and put into operation in September 1980 and they are planned to operate for a test period of at least two years, at the Jutland Telephone Co. head office. This paper gives an impression of the insolation conditions in Denmark and describes briefly the theoretical systems analysis which has formed the basis of the dimensioning of the two pilot plants. Furthermore it describes the principal components of the pilot plants and the goals which the project group has in mind.

articleTitle: Managed Load Distribution
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Annual AC power costs can be reduced by operating power plant rectifiers at their most efficient level. Many electronic switching system (ESS) power plants are operating today at very low efficiency levels due to over engineering as a result of ill-defined drains when these systems were first introduced. Today's state of the art switching equipment is more compact and generally requires less power to operate. Even as new switching equipment is added in offices powered by these older plants, the original calculated drain still will probably never be reached. These plants are the express concern of this paper. The changing energy situation warrants a close look at the power required by these plants. The solution? Power engineers have to adjust these plants to a more efficient operating level. When plants are set to their most efficient operating point, a savings of from two to six percent may be realized. The first part of this paper will deal with the typical rectifier found in the ESS power plant, while the second part will detail the actual adjustments required to obtain the calculated savings.

articleTitle: State of the Art of Mobile and Transportable Power Supplies used in Commercial Power Failure and Emergency in NTT
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: This paper describes the basic philosophy for giving a position and a role in NTT power plant reliability system to mobile and transportable power supply equipment, which are important components in NTT communications power supply system. This paper also introduces equipment configurations.

articleTitle: A Solar Power System for a Microwave Terminal Site
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The Lorain Products Corporation, Division of Reliance Electric, has designed, built and installed a photovoltaic energy conversion system as the prime source of power for a microwave terminal site in Appleton City, Missouri, U.S.A. The basic components of the system are the solar array, the power board, and the battery plant. The raw DC voltage and current generated by the solar array is conditioned by high-efficiency, high-frequency voltage regulators and stored in the battery plant. During periods of darkness or low insolation the battery plant provides power for the microwave equipment load. Peculiar to this solar power system is a special battery charging scheme which very efficiently transfers solar energy to the battery plant and the load, while preventing overcharging and excessive gassing of the batteries. During the charging cycle, digital control circuitry monitors battery response to system charging techniques and adjusts charge voltage and current according to battery requirements and available solar energy. The three controlled voltage regulators, one per sub-array, are capable of applying either an equalize or float voltage to the batteries, and capable of restricting battery charging current, in response to commands from the digital control circuitry. System metering includes an instantaneous indication of battery state-of-charge and provides for the automatic activation of commercially powered standby rectifiers in the event that battery state-of-charge decreases to a predetermined low level. Extended alarms and status indicators are provided for remote monitoring of system operation.

articleTitle: Telephone Central Office Power System Availability
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Switching systems are specified as having a downtime of 2 hours in 40 years. Part of this downtime is attributable to the power system. If the power system contributes 10% of the allowed downtime, then the total power system must meet a downtime requirement of 1 hour in 200 years. This paper will look at the various parts of a telephone power system and determine a reasonable downtime based on failure and repair rates of the various components: 1) ac mains 2) ac standby 3) rectifiers 4) lead acid storage batteries The paper will consider several unusual complications of the power system over other systems with regard to availability as follows: 1) the batteries which provide a limited time reserve redundancy for other failures; 2) the repair rate for ac main recoveries and rectifier and ac standby equipment is not constant - an important factor when coupled with the limited reserve time of the battery; 3) a common fault could conceivably damage more than one rectifier at one time, resulting in a multiple failure; 4) ac standby and battery may fail and not be detected until it is needed.

articleTitle: A Stored-Program Controlled TRIPORT UPS
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The TRIPORT is a single-phase ac uninterruptible power supply, or UPS. This new TRIPORT design employs an eight-bit microprocessor to administer the control functions, perform signal monitoring, and provide self-contained fault diagnostics. The new TRIPORT uses the flexibility of the microcomputer architecture to achieve a control concept applicable to various combinations of input and output voltages and power levels. This paper describes the benefits of stored-program control as applied to the TRIPORT UPS, and the resulting new control techniques and features.

articleTitle: Where the Power Goes
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: This paper looks at the changes in power requirements as communication systems developed and identifies the power losses in the various major building blocks of a telecommunications system. It highlights the cumulative effect of losses in power plant and ancillary equipment for ventilation and cooling and shows where maximum savings of energy could be achieved. The capital and running costs of ancillary plant and necessary buildings have been included in the considerations of energy costs and are expressed in terms of either equivalent energy cost surcharge or as equivalent capital available at installation stage.

articleTitle: Worth of a Watt - Further Insights
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: This paper extends the "worth of a watt" analysis presented during INTELEC 78 which allows equipment designers to estimate the worth of energy used in Bell System central offices. First, the results are shown to be relatively insensitive to the underlying inflation rate of the economy, but depend on an estimate of the relative inflation rate of the cost of electric energy. Then, FETs are examined to show that chip area can be selected for minimal life cycle cost, and that this cost is expected to become lower than that of Schottky diodes as the technology of FETs matures.

articleTitle: Special Requirements to Batteries Applied in Photovoltaic and Wind Power Systems for Telecommunications
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The energy requirements of the loads connected to power supply systems drawing the energy from permanent sources, such as sun or wind, may differ strongly. By defining a rated power of the supply system to which the average power demand of loads can be matched, requirements to the supply system and to its components can be specified. respective results are given for the storage battery. A simple method for sizing the solar generator and the battery is presented. The use of additional power supplies in order to cut down the costs of the systems is discussed. Finally useful electronic components are briefly described. An outlook to the future is given.

articleTitle: High-Frequency Inverter by Reverse-Conducting Thyristors for High-Power Ultrasonic Generator
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: This paper describes some transient and steady-state analyses and the design procedure of a resonance type high-frequency inverter by reverse-conducting thyristors for use with a high-power ultrasonic generator. In the first place, some basic features of the high-frequency inverter treated here are mentioned and these stable oscillation boundary regions are elucidated in connection with theory and experiments. In the second place, transient-state performances are evaluated herein. In the third place, some characteristics for stable operation are illustrated in the relations of some normalized circuit constants and operating frequency. Finally, the circuit design procedure and design example are proposed on the basis of transient and steady-state analyses. The trial high-power ultrasonic generator is concretely demonstrated.

articleTitle: A Modular Power Conditioning System for Computer Power Protection
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The advent of smaller computer systems which consume less power has prompted a reevaluation of power protection. This paper addresses a new power equipment development which combines power protection and power distribution into a single modular unit. This paper presents statistical data regarding power problems and the types of power protection currently being implemented for new generation computers. The use of solid-state, uninterruptible power supply systems cannot be justified for all critical applications. Unique application of a rotary power conditioning system, with outage protection up to 500 milliseconds, is presented in detail. For loads up to 50 kva the motor generator set, power distribution panelboard and power monitoring system can be combined in a single portable package. Operating and performance characteristics for this system are described. The economics of power protection are presented in light of the rapidly declining cost of computer systems. The actual costs of different degrees of power protection are examined.

articleTitle: Power System Availability Performance vs Overall Cost
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The power systems in a time division telecommunication network fall into two categories. The great number of small power equipment feeding concentrators constitute the mainn bulk of maintenance cost and should therefore be optimized for a minimum life cycle cost. The power systems of central switching stations should be designed for maximum availability performance because of the extremely severe effects of power outage. To satisfy the need of quantitative availability performance data, an analysis method is presented, which gives the mean time between system failures and mean down time as a function of the reliability and maintainability performances of power system components and the maintenance support performance. The analysis reveals that the dominant path to system failure will be via dormant faults in batteries, stand-by units or alarm and signalling circuits. This result is confirmed by field data, almost every system failure was an outcome of lacking alarm information. The most dominant rectifier failure cause in rural areas was the lightning originated surge voltage, which also influences the choice of system configuration.

articleTitle: Development and Experience of U.P.S. Systems During the 1970's
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The year 1980 marks the end of a decade, which has seen the development of Uninterruptible Power Systems (U.P.S.) from a laboratory design to a commodity item. This presentation looks back at the major circuits which have been employed, and gives reasons why some have not survived. Failure statistics are given for a recent design to illustrate the state of the art.

articleTitle: Recording and Computerizing DC Distribution Power Drains as Related to Central Office Usage (CCS)
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: This paper describes a method for determining the actual ampere current drain in individual Direct Current (DC) distribution systems. This drain can be obtained as an absolute value, or as a function of central office usage. Analysis indicates that with the use of accurate drain data, the need for additional copper in the form of DC power cables will be greatly reduced, resulting in large capital savings to the telephone companies.

articleTitle: On the Compensation for Cross-Regulation Errors in a Forward DC-DC Converter
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Multi-output dc-dc converters using the cross-regulation method are widely used to provide several regulated and isolated dc output voltages. However, due to the internal resistances and the leakage inductances of the reactor, there appear some steady-state errors on the cross-regulated output voltages. This paper presents a new method to compensate these cross-regulation errors by employing the auxiliary switching transistors in the cross-regulated output circuits, and describes the analysis of its steady-state characteristics and frequency responses in case of two out-put forward converter.

articleTitle: FET Switching Devices for Powering of Telecommunications Circuits
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The low on resistance of the powerfet makes it uniquely suited for energy efficient low voltage applications. The little publicized inverse, gated, mode provides a junction drop free rectifier which is surge current rugged. Gate control by a photovoltaic source is described. Circuit application examples are given. The emerging features of powerfets are of special interest to the telecommunications power circuits designed for long life of service. This is so since the on resistance and hence the power loss, (lifecycle cost of operation) in the FET device trades roughly linearly against the silicon area used (first cost). Typical device parameters are at the present: R<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">on</inf> 50-100 milliohms, switching in tens of nanoseconds, 5-10 volt control of a low leakage gate capacitor.

articleTitle: Quality of the DC Power Supply for Modern Telecommunication Systems
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Quality can be defined as "fitness for purpose". With all telecommunications equipment in a modern UK centre powered from the -48V dc power supply, it has to be of a specified quality. Any unspecified characteristics could cause widespread misoperation or damage. A new dc distribution system has been developed, primarily for new equipment systems which deploy large numbers of dc-dc switching converters. Such equipment is inherently tolerant of wide input voltage limits and low frequency noise voltages but is intolerant of high-energy voltage transients. An investigation has been carried out to restate the critical factors affecting the design of equipment on both sides of the power supply interface.

articleTitle: New Ultrasonic-Frequency Switching-Mode DC-DC Thyristor Converters with Energy Storage Capacitor or Inductor Links
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: This paper presents the latest hardware and application technologies on high-power high-frequency switching-mode step-up-down dc-dc converters by recent high-speed thyristors, which are basically concerned with capacitive energy-or inductive energy-conditioning and processing and their control strategies. New quick-response dc-dc power converters proposed conveniently are effectively suitable for large-capacity telecommunication energy processing system and solar energy processing plant and so forth. The practical capacitive energy storage types and inductive energy storage types of high-power switching-mode dc-dc converters by high-frequency switching techniques are concretely demonstrated by experimental model equipments and discussed from some comparative studies between dc-dc converters mentioned above.

articleTitle: Power Feeding and Personal Safety in Cable Transmission Systems
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The repeaters in telecommunication cables are power fed. Currents of up to 0,5 amperes flow at potentials of up to several hundred volts. To ensure that no one is injured if he touches the projecting live conductor when working on an undamaged or damaged cable, even if the power feeding is switched on, such circuits are designed with the following considerations in mind: The power-feeding circuit is symmetrical and is balanced to ground with high impedance at the feeding point only. The switch-attachment needed in any case for fault location for every repeater ensure that the contact voltage remain harmless and low in the event of a fault. Power-feeding terminations are available for rendering the work site safe when lengthy work on the cable is necessary and transmission has to be simultaneously maintained.

articleTitle: Forward Converters Operating Directly off the Three Phase Rectified Mains Suitable for Exchange Use
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Current developments in the components for high voltage switching power supplies now permit operation directly from the three phase rectified mains supply. In particular, the basic performance requirements will be given for modular telecommunications power plant with particular reference to the external performance parameters e.g. ripple, noise. efficiency. General solutions will be given and also from a comparison of the relative merits of these a specific design will be detailed. Particular reference will be made to alternative solutions to the various problems met with in switching power supply design.

articleTitle: Emergency Generators in Public Exchanges
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The generators considered are of the solid state brushless exciter type, rated 50 kVA to 500 kVA. The following aspects relevant to the selection of emergency generators and to the design of installations fed by these generators will be described: 1. Different types of generators available. 2. Differences between the standards of VDE, BS, NEMA, IEC. 3. Protection of the generator and the installation. Factors arising from the different fault characteristics of generators and transformers. 4. Considerations pertaining to motor starting. 5. Influence of the harmonic distortion, caused by the rectifiers, on induction motor losses.

articleTitle: Power Engineering and Operational Reviews
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Power Engineering and Operational Reviews are being implemented for the power systems in telephone central office buildings primarily to improve preparedness for commercial power failures and to improve engineering and utilization of power equipment in the most cost effective manner. The need for the program is brought on by increased dependence on less reliable commercial power, the trend toward unattended operation and to improve engineering and maintenance of power systems. Procedures for making Reviews are covered.

articleTitle: A Newcomer in Energy Storage : The ACE
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Derived from space technologies that are being applied for optimized momentum or inertia flywheels within satellite attitude control systems, a kinetic energy storage unit has been developed by Company Aerospatiale. Main features of this unit are an electro-magnetic suspension system, a motor-generator of 3 KW power, a heavy steel rotor storing 1 KWh useful energy, placed inside a vacuum container, and the associated electronics. This device offers attractive technical characteristics and is being tested by the French telephone administration (CNET) in view of its application as a back up energy source. Other units, of larger capacities, and other utilisations, are under preparation.

articleTitle: Lead-Acid Battery Selection for Electronic Switching
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: In considering the maximum and minimum permissable voltages on any DC power system for telephone power use it is necessary to review the designs of switching equipment that have been available for the past 30 years. Over the years the most common number of hours used in calculating the capacity of batteries has been 8 hours. This was predicted on overall telephone systems: center city, urban, and rural. And superimposed on this 8 hour duration was an allowance for "busy hour" operation of the batteries. Since the early 1960s the alloys used in the design of both "antimony" and "calcium" batteries have been changing to keep pace with the improved grid casting techniques and with the increased life expectancy of flat plate batteries. At the commencement of the design change under consideration, flat plate battery systems had a life expectancy of around 12 years. Today this has been improved by rigid control of grain size and alloy content to more than 20 years. This has reduced float current which in turn has demanded the use of higher floating voltages to insure that sufficient floating current is drawn into the battery to maintain its operating stability. To obtain the full life expectancy from any of the products there is a restriction on the number of equivalent 8 hour discharges per year. For guidance we provide a table giving the overall comparisons of the four industries telephone batteries available.

articleTitle: The Effect of Refrigeration Compressor Operation on the Economy of Heat Recovery
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: In conventional environmental control by air conditioning, independent systems of heating and cooling are used, one consuming energy to provide heat whilst the other uses energy to reject it. If both systems are called upon to operate at the same time there is scope for recovering the waste heat from the cooling plant and re-using it for space or water heating. This Paper shows that where compression refrigeration is used, the temperature of the heat source should be limited for economic reasons.

articleTitle: Self-Oscillating Polyphase Inverter with Current Feedback
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: A three-phase self-oscillating inverter of reduced volume and minimal phase-distortion is proposed. To reduce core size, a diode-bridge and a common resistance are inserted in the control source for the saturable cores. The windings of the saturable cores are ring-connected to effectively improve the phase distortion and the stability. The oscillation frequency is derived analytically and methods to control the frequency are discussed. The effect of the current feedback is investigated for the case in which the induction motor is driven by this three-phase inverter.

articleTitle: Wind Electric Systems for Telecommunications
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The rapidly expanding demand for communications services in remote areas of the world coupled to rising fuel costs has generated a critical need for a reliable alternative to fossil fuel based primary power supplies. Wind Energy Conversion Systems (WECS) have been solving remote power needs since the turn of the century. However, until recently very little hardware was available which was designed and manufactured specifically to meet the severe reliability and environmental requirements of the telecommunications industry. Recognizing this deficiency, the U.S. Department of Energy in 1978 awarded a contract to North Wind Power Company to design, test, and deliver a small high reliability wind energy conversion system capable of producing economical power from the wind in the harshest of environments with a mean time between failures of no less than 10 years on a maintenance schedule of no more than one day per year. This paper describes the result of that effort, the North Wind Power HR2 wind electric system and discusses the feasibility and economics of such a wind system as a primary power source for remote telecommunications applications.

articleTitle: Table of Content
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference

articleTitle: Parallel UPS Control and Configuration
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The Multimodule Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) has been accepted as the most reliable power source. For further reliability improvement a parallel-redundant configuration is frequently used. The first principle of redundancy requires the elimination of points common to all modules. The second requires the availability of the redundant logic, to remove the faulty unit off line without affecting the others. Parallel operation in multi-module system is well described by L.H. Walker (1), with some systems considerations by Goodwin (3). This paper is an extension of the above publications with emphasis on development of control schemes currently used in some parallel redundant configurations. Two load sharing loop configurations are discussed, along with the behaviour of the circulation current under different fault condition. Special attention is given to the selective trip funtion. It is proven that a load sharing loop can be used as a source of necessary information required to remove the faulty unit off line. The presented method can also be used for a selective trip for over or under-frequency conditions of two or multi-module systems. The discussed method does sot employ control hardware except for the load sharing loop which is triplicated for redundancy.

articleTitle: A Microprocessor-Based PWM Controller for DC/AC Inverters
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference

articleTitle: Synthesised Computer Power, Its Application, Monitoring and Distribution
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The proliferation of computer installations, the drive towards lower cost computer systems and the increasing range of non-computer equipment causing power disturbances, all create pressures for the introduction of improved computer power conditioning equipment to ensure trouble-free computer operation. Recent Computer Industry developments in this field take the form of packaged Static Power Synthesis systems, offering convenient and economical power conditioning and distribution facilities, with monitoring which permits the computer user to control his power environment.

articleTitle: The Power Requirements of the Programme Chain
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The paper outlines the structure of programme contribution and distribution arrangements for the radio and television networks of the British Broadcasting Corporation. It elaborates on the electrical power supply requirements at key points in the programme chain and the BBC's approach to meeting them. Special design features of power equipment used for outside broadcasts, at studio centres and at transmitting stations are considered.

articleTitle: A New Power System for TD-2 Microwave Radio
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: With the evolution of TD-2 Radio into a completely solid-state system, a new powering arrangement was introduced to reduce power plant maintenance and battery replacement costs, to lower energy costs, and to allow recovery of floor space in existing repeater stations, a factor vital to radio overbuild* programs.

articleTitle: Planté - "An Old Dog with New Tricks"
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Traditional and modern Planté cells are used to provide a high integrity source of standby power in the telecommunications industry because of their long and predictable life, stability on float charge, low maintenance and reliable performance. In addition, their high rate performance has made them suitable for generating station applications such as switch and circuit breaker tripping, together with diesel and gas turbine starting operations. In recent times, planté cells have found applications in the important and growing fields of uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and solarvoltaic systems. Each new application has been accompanied, to some extent, by design modifications which have enabled the product to be closely matched to the requirements of the application. This evolution is reviewed in the light of the special requirements of certain applications, and with particular reference to power density. Today's Planté Cells for UPS applications offer significant reductions in floor space requirements and some battery cost savings. Improvements in performance have not been achieved, however, to the detriment of life and reliability.

articleTitle: Lead Acid Standby Power Batteries in Telecommunications - "Horses for Courses"
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: A review is made of the battery applications in the Telecommunications Industry and of the various types of lead acid battery currently in use. Network Switching applications use all the three basic types of lead acid battery (Plante, Tubular and Pasted Plate) and this situation is accounted for in terms of the mutual development of the system and its battery in close co-operation between user and manufacturer. Performance selective applications such as Engine Starting and Uninterrupted Power Supplies requiring fast rates of discharge are discussed and a case is made out, in certain circumstances, for selecting the Plante cell for the optimum battery system. Design selective applications are discussed and the Tubular cell battery is identified as the natural choice for Maritime Installations (Oil Rigs) and cells with large electrolyte reserves to be used in batteries for Solar Power systems. Trends for the future of lead acid batteries are considered and this is related to the need for International Standardisation.

articleTitle: Standby Diesel Power Generation and Associated Control Equipment
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The paper covers factors which determine the requirement for a standby system in telecommunications centres and which affect the design of the system. Details of diesel generating set characteristics are given in relation to standby system design parameters and environmental limitations. Engine systems design is described, including controls as engineered for sets recently supplied by APE-Allen to British Post Office Telecommunications.

articleTitle: Selection Criteria for Diesel Cranking Batteries
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Selection of batteries for starting of diesel engines comprises both the choice of an appropriate battery type and a correct size, having in mind that economy and reliability should be considered along with technical performance. The power requirements for starting depend i.a. on motor size, required cranking speed, motor oil grade and temperature. The influence of these factors on the battery demands are discussed, and simple design relationships are derived. Having established the appropriate selection criteria in view of engine specifications and environmental conditions, the most common cranking battery types are discussed. Each type is assigned a figure of merit, taking price, performance and life expectancy into account. It is concluded that lead-acid batteries with tubular positive plates offer the best economy, except under extreme environmental conditions.

articleTitle: Determining the Optimum Thermal Design of Buildings Housing Telecommunications Switching Equipment
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The necessity to conserve diminishing energy resources has prompted a recent upgrading of that section of the UK Building Regulations covering the allowable thermal transmittance value (U-value) of the building fabric. External walls, exposed floors and roofs should not now exceed a U-value of 0.6 W/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. °C. Such a restriction if applied to telecommunications buildings housing switching equipment with high internal heat gains will in fact have the effect of increasing the energy consumption and running costs of the air conditioning plant. A computer model to determine the optimum U-value (ie. minimum air conditioning plant running costs) for such buildings has been developed and is presented in this paper.

articleTitle: Technologies and Future Trends in Rectifiers for Customer Premises Telecommunications Equipment
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Rectifiers for Bell System customer premises telecommunications equipment such as Private Automatic Branch Exchanges (PABX or PBX), key telephone systems (KTS), and data sets employ a variety of technologies. That variety includes linear transformers, ferroresonant transformers, and, in a few instances, line rectifiers followed by dc-dc converters. For multiple output rectifiers, these technologies are combined with linear regulators and/or switching regulators to control most or all outputs. In the United States, a 60-Hz ferroresonant transformer is frequently used to eliminate problems caused by lightning strikes on the ac feeders, or surges caused by load changes or source switching on these feeders. Lightning strikes and voltage surges can be mitigated by other means, however, thus allowing designers to apply many of the techniques used in dc-dc converters operating above 20 kHz, to rectifiers connected to ac sources of 50 or 60 Hz. This paper discusses circuit topologies for such high frequency power supplies as well as methods for overcurrent limiting, inrush current limiting, overvoltage protection, and mechanical packages to meet unusual thermal and mechanical constraints.

articleTitle: Modular Power Supply Equipment in the French Telecommunications Network
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: This article presents a range of power supply units used for electronic satellite exchanges having a capacity of less than 8000 subscriber lines. A modular design is used and all converters use high frequency (f ⩾ 20 kHz) for DC switching transistors. A short description of the modules and interfacing equipment will be found, followed by some comments on the benefits of this new equipment for network operation.

articleTitle: Operating Experience with Secured Power Supply Systems Comprising Standby Diesel Driven Generating Sets and Rectifier/Charger Units with Batteries
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Different designs of secured or no-break emergency power-supply systems for a.c. or d.c. are in use to ensure continuity of load power in case of mains outages or faults in power generating and distribution systems. Static power supply systems with batteries for energy storage are often supplied by mains or diesel emergency generating sets to tide them over mains outages. This is to reduce the necessary battery stored-energy time; or else to continue operation beyond the installed battery stored-energy time in case of extended faults in primary power supply. With such combinations of diesel standby generators with static secured power supplies, difficulties may occur under certain circumstances by oscillations at generator frequency and power or by harmonic feedback from the rectifiers. Some aspects of these difficulties, and means to overcome them are discussed.

articleTitle: Primary Switched Power Supplies with Ferroresonant Stabilization
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Primary switched power supplies operating at supersonic conversion frequencies (20-50 kHz) are usually based on duty cycle control. This paper presents another possible technique - ferroresonant control. The difficulties connected with the application of the ferroresonant principle at high frequencies can be eliminated by using the controlled ferroresonant technique. The paper covers the principle of operation and the evaluation of the performance of ferroresonant control, as compared with switched-mode duty-cycle-controlled devices. A practical implementation, a unit of 175 W output power, is described and its performance presented.

articleTitle: Photovoltaic Power Supplies for Telecommunication Systems in Remote Areas
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Currently most low powered telecommunication systems (such as VHF radiotelephone systems, high capacity microwave telephone and television repeaters etc.) in remote areas are powered by conventional stand alone power supplies which include: conventional batteries, diesel motor/generator sets and small gas turbines; with associated fuel transportation and regular maintenance costs. With the requirements of reliable, low maintenance power sources for remote telecommunication systems, photovoltaic power supplies are becoming a viable and for low loads (up to 200 W continuous and more) a preferred power supply for remote areas. However, the wide-spread use of pv power supplies for such applications depend on: a) pv system economic competition which includes lowering of solar cell panel prices as well as balance of system components (power conditioning, batteries etc.). b) Improved system design and more field experience under real conditions. The first part of this paper reports briefly the present R & D activities of AEG-TELEFUNKEN in developing pv power supplies for remote communication systems which include the automated techniques for pv panel production using 10 × 10 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> multicrystalline SI-cells as well as optimized component development. The second part gives the description of various systems installed for powering several isolated communication systems such as radio telephone, transmitters and relay stations.

articleTitle: Wind Energy for Remote Telecommunications Power
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: Technological developments of small wind energy conversion systems have accelerated in the post decade. These systems are being evaluated for their technical feasibility, competitive costs of electric power generation, high reliability of design and performance, and minimal environmental impact. Small wind energy conversion systems are commercially available and, for select applications, are cost competitive. They have been used to provide electric power in remote areas where access to an electric distribution grid is too difficult or expensive. Small wind energy conversion systems will play an important role in the developmental process in selected countries. As microwave repeater stations expand into underpopulated regions they will require their own power source. Small wind energy conversion systems are presented as a technology appropriate for this application.

articleTitle: The Heemaf Dynamic Diesel UPS System
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: In the Heemaf dynamic diesel UPS-system a tapped choke coil and a free running synchronous a.c. machine act as a filter for transients, higher harmonics, peaks, and voltage variations in the mains power supply. In addition, the a.c. machine drives an induction coupling with a high speed rotor which stores the energy required to supply power to the load during the starting time of the diesel engine. This principle results in improved efficiency and reliability in comparison with more conventional UPS-systems. Heemaf diesel UPS-systems can be supplied in ratings from 100 kVA up to 500 kVA for single sets, while for sets operating in parallel ratings in excess of 2000 kVA are possible.

articleTitle: A Microcomputer Controlled Diesel Engine Generator
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: This paper shows that a microcomputer can control and diagnose a single standby diesel engine generator. Calculations show that high reliability is achieved when maintenance is conducted at short intervals and complete repair is performed. The hardware and software of a diesel engine generator equipped with a microcomputer controller, together with results of environment test, are introduced.

articleTitle: Energy Conservation in the Bell System
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The Nation and telecommunications systems are confronted with a continuing energy problem resulting from limited resources to meet an ever increasing demand. The Bell System provides numerous examples of ways in which demand for energy may be reduced, resulting in conservation of resources and preservation of the environment. The Bell System provides a telecommunications network linking nearly 185 million telephones and handling in excess of 790 million calls a day. In providing telecommunications services, the Bell System employs more than one million people, utilizes almost 30,000 buildings, and operates more than 195,000 motor vehicles (the world's largest owned and operated private fleet). However, the Bell System is not energy intensive. It uses only about one tenth of one percent of the Nation's energy, while contributing over two percent of the gross national product. Following the 1973 oil embargo, the Bell System applied its full resources to determine and implement ways of conserving energy. In 1980, the Bell System used 10% less energy than in this period of 1973, while the volume of business increased 73% and the number of telephones in service increased more than 30%. As a result of energy conservation, 30% less energy was used in 1980 than would have been used without energy conservation. The Companies of the Bell System have an energy budget commitment objective to use significantly less energy in 1986 than was used in 1973.

articleTitle: Features and Requirements Concerning Reliability of DC Power Supply for Telecommunications
publicationTitle: INTELEC '81 - Third International Telecommunications Energy Conference
abstract: The known publications concerning reliability in DC Power Plants have been either superficial or restricted to a few specific sets of devices (e.g. rectifiers, converters), what implies in misleading and other inadequacies. The paper aims at divulging the results of studies and researches as to reliability, held in Brazil, which were the basis for the definitions regarding the standardization of Primary DC Power Plants for all the Brazilian Telecommunication Companies forming the TELEBRAS Group. A consistent analysis is made to deter mine the overall power feeding reliability taking into account all the important factors involved. Suitable approaches are made regarding assessment of some parameters such as: time for failure detection (t<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">d</inf>); probability of failure in the starting of an emergency AC generator (or any other device which either does not operate continuously or has no self-supervision); factor of success in repairing proceeding as a function of battery autonomy period.
